subtitle: How to say a computer is “fast” with a number, and what the processor actually does between two ticks.

orgarch.body:
Two cars can look identical from the driver’s seat yet have very different engines. Computers are the same, and the field draws a careful line between what you see and what is under the bonnet. Computer architecture is what a programmer can see: the instruction set, registers, addressing modes and data types. Computer organisation is how it is built to provide that: control signals, buses, cache design, the technology. Two machines with the same architecture (two x86 chips) can have very different organisations, and different speeds.

At the top level a computer is a processor that fetches instructions and data from memory, with I/O to the outside world, joined by a bus. A multi-core processor simply puts several processors on one chip sharing the memory system. In the figure, the three buses carry addresses, data and control signals. So if two processors run the same programs but one is faster, what differs? The organisation.
keynotes: Computer architecture is what a programmer can see: instruction set, registers, addressing modes and data types.
Computer organisation is how it is built: control signals, buses, cache design and technology.
A computer is a processor, memory and I/O joined by a bus; a multi-core processor puts several processors on one chip sharing the memory system.

cycle.body:
Your processor does one small thing, over and over, billions of times a second. Every instruction goes through the same loop: fetch it from the address in the program counter, decode what it asks for, execute it (possibly fetching operands and writing a result), then advance the program counter. A jump simply loads a new address into the counter, and interrupts are checked between instructions.

Watch an Intel 8085 do exactly this: each step is one instruction, the highlighted row is the one about to run, and the registers and flags change beneath. The example adds 25H + 17H, and the result 3CH lands in memory at 2052H. After a normal (non-jump) instruction executes, the program counter simply advances to the next instruction.
keynotes: Every instruction goes through fetch (from the address in the program counter), decode, execute, then advance the program counter.
A jump loads a new address into the program counter; interrupts are checked between instructions.
In the 8085 example 25H + 17H gives 3CH, stored in memory at 2052H.

perf.body:
“This computer is fast” is not a number. To compare machines honestly you need a formula, and you should know it by heart: execution time = instruction count × CPI (cycles per instruction) × clock period. The clock rate is only one of the three factors; a faster clock with a worse CPI can be slower. MIPS = instruction count / (time × 10⁶) = clock rate / (CPI × 10⁶), but MIPS misleads across different instruction sets.

Run it once. A 2 GHz processor runs a program of 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5. Cycles = instructions × CPI, and time = cycles / clock, so t = (10⁹ × 1.5)/(2 × 10⁹) = 0.75 s. And MIPS = 2000/1.5 ≈ 1333. Now a puzzle for you: a compiler change cuts the instruction count by 20% but raises CPI by 30%. Multiply the factors, 0.8 × 1.3 = 1.04, so the program gets slightly slower.
keynotes: Execution time = instruction count × CPI × clock period; clock rate is only one of the three factors.
MIPS = instruction count / (time × 10⁶) = clock rate / (CPI × 10⁶), but it misleads across different instruction sets.
A 2 GHz processor running 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5 takes 0.75 s, which is about 1333 MIPS.

amdahl.body:
Suppose you hire ten cooks for a recipe. Does dinner arrive ten times sooner? Not if one step, like waiting for the oven, cannot be shared. Amdahl’s law puts a number on it: speeding up only a fraction f of a program by a factor s gives overall speed-up 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s). The serial part (1 − f) caps everything: even with infinite s the limit is 1/(1 − f).

Try it. A program spends 80% of its time in a part that can be made 4× faster (f = 0.8, s = 4). Then the speed-up = 1/(0.2 + 0.8/4) = 1/0.4 = 2.5. This is why adding cores helps only a little for mostly-serial programs. If 10% of a program is serial, the maximum speed-up with unlimited processors is 1/0.1 = 10.
keynotes: Speeding up a fraction f of a program by a factor s gives overall speed-up 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s).
The serial part (1 − f) caps everything: even with infinite s the limit is 1/(1 − f).
With f = 0.8 and s = 4 the speed-up is 1/(0.2 + 0.8/4) = 2.5.

risc.body:
There are two schools of thought about how to design an instruction set, and you will meet both in your career. CISC machines (x86) have many complex, variable-length instructions, some of which do a lot of work. RISC machines (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) have few, simple, fixed-length instructions, use load/store for all memory access and keep many registers, which makes pipelining easy.

Berkeley RISC added a neat trick, overlapped register windows: each procedure gets a window of registers that overlaps its caller’s, so parameters are passed without touching memory. In the figure, the complexity lives in microcode (CISC) or in the compiler (RISC). Why do RISC processors allow only load/store instructions to touch memory? So that all the other instructions are simple, uniform and fast to pipeline.
keynotes: CISC machines (x86) have many complex, variable-length instructions; RISC machines (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) have few, simple, fixed-length instructions and use load/store for all memory access.
RISC keeps many registers, which makes pipelining easy.
Berkeley RISC added overlapped register windows so parameters pass without touching memory.

summary.body:
Four lines are all you need to take away.

  • Architecture = visible contract; organisation = implementation.
  • Time = instructions × CPI × period.
  • Amdahl: the serial fraction limits speed-up.
  • The instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute, repeat.
keynotes: Architecture is the visible contract and organisation is the implementation.
Time = instructions × CPI × period, and Amdahl says the serial fraction limits speed-up.
The instruction cycle is fetch, decode, execute, repeat.
